summary: Gives an overview of the High-level Entity Management System (HEMS), an experimental system for managing hosts, gateways and other network entities. It was being tested in parts of the Internet at the time. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a plan for a remote control panel that lets people check on and adjust the computers and routers on a network from afar.

questions: how was network management done before snmp
what is the high-level entity management protocol
subtitle: An overview of an experimental system for monitoring and controlling gateways, hosts and other IP network devices.

tldr.problem: The number of vendors of network components had grown and there was no accepted standard for managing them, making management of the growing Internet very difficult.
tldr.mechanism: HEMS has a small query processor and an event generator on each managed entity, plus applications that send queries over the High-Level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP) using self-describing ASN.1 data, with several instructions allowed per message.
tldr.outcome: The system was experimental and meant to lead to a standard for IP internetwork management. It is now Historic.

today: RFC 1021 is Historic. It described an experimental system, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The related parts are in RFC 1022, RFC 1023 and RFC 1024.

sections.title: Why a Management System
sections.content:
Until recently, a majority of critical components in IP networks, such as gateways, came from a small set of vendors, each with its own management protocols. An administrator could learn them all. As the number of vendors grew, and with the explosive growth of the Internet, the lack of an accepted standard caused severe management problems.

The memo is an overview of the RFCs that make up the High-Level Entity Management System: this memo plus RFC 1022, RFC 1024 and RFC 1023. It is experimental, was being tested in portions of the Internet, and was hoped to help lead to a standard for IP internetwork management.

It splits management into monitoring (collecting data to observe behavior) and control (taking actions to change behavior). Control presupposes monitoring and is harder to define, so the authors concentrated on monitoring. Several control components, such as strong access control, were not fully defined.
sections.plainLanguage: When many different kinds of network machines each need their own special tools, nobody can manage them all. HEMS tried to give them one shared way to be checked on.

sections.title: Query Processor, Events and Applications
sections.content:
HEMS has three parts: a query processor that can live on any addressable entity, an event generator on entities, and applications that send requests and interpret replies. The query processor interprets all monitoring and control requests. It was designed to be as small and simple as management requirements allow, so that it would be widely implemented, while remaining extensible, robust and independent of host architecture.

Objects are self-describing, using the binary encoding of ISO ASN.1 (a limited subset, so handling can be optimized). A message may hold multiple instructions, which the authors expected to be faster than a remote procedure system limited to one operation per message. Every entity manages a small standard set of objects, entity types such as gateways may need more, and entities may offer extra ones that can be discovered.

Events are unsolicited status messages, called traps in the IP community. They are handled as specialized replies, sent to one or more management centers, in ASN.1 with well-known codes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device has a little helper that answers questions and can also shout when something happens. A manager program does the thinking and showing.

sections.title: The Protocol and Its Transport
sections.content:
Query processors and applications talk using the High-Level Entity Management Protocol (HEMP), which defines the format of queries and replies. HEMP runs over a standard transport protocol, and the memo explains why one choice does not fit all uses. It expects three kinds of activity: status monitoring, firefighting and event reporting.

Status monitoring on a healthy network could use an unreliable transport. Firefighting, when packets are being lost, needs a reliable protocol so diagnostic data and control requests get through. Events need not be reliable, since a serious problem will recur and send the event again, and they often go to several centers, which rules out a connection-oriented protocol like TCP.

Two transport options were chosen: the experimental Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP) for more experimental systems, and a combination of TCP and UDP for near-term production systems, as described in RFC 1022.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network is fine, a quick postcard is enough. When it is broken, you need registered mail so the message really arrives.

sections.title: Compatibility With CMIP
sections.content: Several groups wanted applications that work with both HEMS and the emerging ISO Common Management Information Protocol (CMIP). At the highest level both perform operations on objects held in remote entities, and both represent those objects with ASN.1. That makes it feasible to build a standard set of interface routines that can reach either system, even though the underlying mechanics are quite different.
sections.plainLanguage: Two systems can speak differently inside yet look alike from outside, so one program can talk to both.

items.title: Query processor
items.text: Interprets monitoring and control requests on an entity.

items.title: Event generator
items.text: Sends unsolicited status messages, called events, to management centers.

items.title: Applications
items.text: Send requests to the query processor and interpret replies.
